Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Places of worship or religious gatherings

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

vignette:
Keilani finds a strange sort of peace in the pre-dawn quiet of the national park, the time before the tourists arrive with their loud voices and bright jackets. For the past six months, since returning from her deployment as a relief worker, these have been the only hours she feels remotely like herself. The woman who once thrived on challenge and human connection now spends her days as a park ranger seeking the most isolated patrol routes, a ghost in the vast wilderness she is meant to protect. Her husband says it’s like living with a stranger, and she knows he is right. The distance between them feels as wide and silent as the valleys she now hides in.

The woman who haunts her had worn a sweet, cloying perfume, something like jasmine. She had arrived at the makeshift clinic with a small child, her eyes wide with a fear Keilani had come to recognize as the baseline state for civilians in the conflict zone. Keilani had been triaging, moving from one person to the next with a forced calm, when the building across the street was hit. The blast threw her against a wall. When the dust settled, the air was thick with screams and the scent of jasmine. The woman was gone, buried under rubble, and her child was clinging to Keilani’s leg, silent and trembling. Keilani had frozen, unable to move or speak, a moment of paralysis she now sees as the ultimate failure. She had acted in a way that went against everything she believed herself to be; she had failed a child when he needed her most.

Now, that scent is a constant threat. Last week, a hiker passed her on the trail, and the light floral perfume she wore sent a jolt of panic through Keilani’s body. The trigger brought not a story, but a sensory snapshot: the smell of jasmine, the rough texture of the child's coat, the taste of dust, and the woman’s terrified eyes just before the blast. The scent didn't just bring back the moment; it brought with it the immediate, visceral certainty that she was still that same failed person, frozen and useless. These moments are intensely clear, while the minutes before and after remain a complete blank. After the memory receded, it left an echo, making her hyper-attuned to the world around her; for hours afterward, any floral scent or the sight of a woman with a child felt like a direct and personal warning. This sudden intrusion of the past immediately prompted her to retreat, turning off the main trail onto an unmarked game path, a strategy of avoidance that is becoming second nature. She finds that the more she avoids people on her patrols, the less chance there is of the memory ambushing her.

This sense of being ambushed has generalized into a constant state of threat. Keilani is now superalert, her body perpetually braced for impact. The sudden flight of a grouse from the undergrowth or the quick, unexpected movement of a tourist raising a camera makes her flinch violently. Living at this constant pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with potential warnings; the scent of a wildflower on the breeze or the sight of a mother adjusting her child's jacket were no longer neutral observations but immediate, personal threats. On days when this feeling of imminent danger was highest, the memory was closest to the surface, as if her mind needed to keep the blueprint of the disaster readily available to prepare for the next one. This pervasive feeling of danger has reinforced her decision to avoid any unfamiliar areas, sticking only to the three patrol routes she knows by heart. Her supervisor has noted her refusal to survey new park sections, a core part of her job she can no longer bring herself to do. The world, even this one of mountains and trees, feels fundamentally unsafe to her.

At the heart of this withdrawal is a set of beliefs that have taken root and grown toxic. Keilani is convinced that her freezing in that moment was a profound moral failing, a violation of her deepest values. This belief that she had betrayed her own code acted like a magnet, constantly pulling her mind back to the sensory fragments of the event, as if reviewing them might somehow change the verdict. This conviction has led her to feel as though she no longer belongs anywhere—not in her marriage, not in her uniform, not in the world of ordinary, unbroken people. Believing herself to be fundamentally broken and a potential danger to others, her systematic withdrawal from social contact and professional responsibilities felt less like a choice and more like a necessary precaution. This appraisal that she is fundamentally damaged and untrustworthy directly fuels her hypervigilance; she feels she must remain on guard at all times to prevent another catastrophic failure. The world is dangerous because she is in it, incompetent and unworthy of her role.

This self-condemnation has become a self-sustaining cycle. Her belief that she is broken makes her hyper-attuned to any reminder of the trauma, which in turn makes the intrusive memories and sensory triggers more frequent and intense. When a memory does break through, it serves as proof of her appraisal that she is damaged beyond repair. In response to these triggers, she has systematically dismantled her life. She avoids crowds, has stopped attending the church she and her husband once found solace in, and refuses to see a doctor for a persistent cough, terrified of any formal setting where her failure might be exposed. The very act of scanning a trail for hikers to avoid, or planning her day around evading populated areas, had the effect of keeping the possibility of encountering a trigger at the forefront of her mind, making her even more sensitive when one inevitably appeared. These acts of avoidance only deepen her conviction that she is an outcast.

The cost has been highest at home. When her husband, desperate to connect, reaches out to hug her, the physical affection is no longer a comfort. It is a trigger, bringing back the suffocating memory of the small child clinging to her leg. She instinctively stiffens and pulls away. This rejection deepens the chasm between them and powerfully confirms her belief that she is unlovable and no longer belongs in her own family. By pushing away comfort and refusing to speak of the event—because when she tries, the thread is lost and she cannot finish the story—she ensures the memory remains a set of terrifying, unprocessed fragments.

It was after spending an entire eight-hour shift unable to leave the cab of her truck, paralyzed by the fear of who she might encounter on the trail, that she knew she could not go on. The thought that her life was not worth living had become a quiet, constant companion. Her husband had made the appointment. Keilani arrived convinced she was beyond help, but with a flicker of hope that she might one day learn how to tell the story of what happened, and in doing so, find a place in the world where she could belong again.

The vignette does not explain how the trauma memory itself makes the patient more sensitive or hyper-attuned to triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not describe an instance where a trigger directly causes or activates a negative appraisal.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not describe the patient's negative appraisals as a direct cause of her intrusive memories.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not explain how the trauma memory itself makes the patient more sensitive or hyper-attuned to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not describe the patient's pervasive sense of threat as a direct cause of her intrusive memories.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not describe how the patient's avoidance behaviors make her more sensitive or hyper-attuned to triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

Believing herself to be fundamentally broken and a potential danger to others, her systematic withdrawal from social contact and professional responsibilities felt less like a choice and more like a necessary precaution. This appraisal that she is fundamentally damaged and untrustworthy directly fuels her hypervigilance; she feels she must remain on guard at all times to prevent another catastrophic failure. The world is dangerous because she is in it, incompetent and unworthy of her role.

This self-condemnation has become a self-sustaining cycle. Her belief that she is broken makes her hyper-attuned to any reminder of the trauma, which in turn makes the intrusive memories and sensory triggers more frequent and intense. When a memory does break through, it serves as proof of her appraisal that she is damaged beyond repair. In response to these triggers, she has systematically dismantled her life. She avoids crowds, has stopped attending the church she and her husband once found solace in, and refuses to see a doctor for a persistent cough, terrified of any formal setting where her failure might be exposed. The very act of scanning a trail for hikers to avoid, or planning her day around evading populated areas, had the effect of keeping the possibility of encountering a trigger at the forefront of her mind, making her even more sensitive when one inevitably appeared. These acts of avoidance only deepen her conviction that she is an outcast.

The cost has been highest at home. When her husband, desperate to connect, reaches out to hug her, the physical affection is no longer a comfort. It is a trigger, bringing back the suffocating memory of the small child clinging to her leg. She instinctively stiffens and pulls away. This rejection deepens the chasm between them and powerfully confirms her belief that she is unlovable and no longer belongs in her own family. By pushing away comfort and refusing to speak of the event—because when she tries, the thread is lost and she cannot finish the story—she ensures the memory remains a set of terrifying, unprocessed fragments.

It was after spending an entire eight-hour shift unable to leave the cab of her truck, paralyzed by the fear of who she might encounter on the trail, that she knew she could not go on. The thought that her life was not worth living had become a quiet, constant companion. Her husband had made the appointment. Keilani arrived convinced she was beyond help, but with a flicker of hope that she might one day learn how to tell the story of what happened, and in doing so, find a place in the world where she could belong again.
